articles.headline: Before the event: what Altico's filings did and did not reveal
articles.dek: A construction-PIT replay of Altico: the first published regulatory or funding signal, the disclosure clock, the miss, and the boundary that survives into today's screen.
articles.body_markdown:
Nothing in today's Failure Radar evidence cleared the bar for a fresh institution story. This is therefore a historical replay, **not current news and not a forecast**. It opens the public Altico record because a quiet daily tape is better used to examine what an early-warning system could actually have known than to manufacture a new alarm.

The recorded outcome date is **2019-09-12**. LiquiLens's reconstruction asks two narrower questions. Did the disclosed ratios enter a published regulatory action zone? Did the disclosed liability structure enter a funding-fragility band? It does not ask whether a modern model, armed with later revisions and hindsight, can draw a persuasive line through the event.

## The record before the event

The first regulatory action-zone row is dated **not observed**, with a conservative knowledge-time proxy of **not available**. Its status is **no action-zone entry in the record**, its breached fields are **none published**, and its recorded lead is **unavailable months**.

The funding replay is independently scoreable: **True**. Its first signal is dated **2017-03-31**, with knowledge-time proxy **2017-05-30**, index **23.7**, band **stable**, flags **CP reliance 29% (rollover-freeze exposure)**, and lead **27 months**.

Those two rows are allowed to disagree. Regulatory thresholds look for capital and asset-quality boundaries. Funding fragility looks for liability dependence and rollover exposure. One can fire while the other stays silent because they describe different failure physics.

## What the lenses saw

The [public replay page](https://liquilens.in/replay/altico/) preserves the observed entries and misses side by side. The regulatory lens reports the institution against the framework's own tripwires. The funding lens requires liability disclosures and abstains when a usable series is absent. The hazard model excludes fraud-masked failures from fitting because fabricated disclosures carry no honest deterioration signal.

Across the full India record, the regulatory replay summary contains **15** failed institutions and **5** first action-zone entries, with a median recorded lead of **41 months**. The funding replay contains **10** institutions with liability disclosures and **4** first funding signals.

Those are diagnostic counts, not a validated backtest. The dossiers use explicit publication time when it exists and otherwise a conservative period-end-plus-filing-lag proxy. The source record says that the missing complete revision archive can make reconstructed lead times optimistic.

## Why the warning mattered

An early warning matters only if it names a mechanism and leaves time to test it. An action-zone breach says capital or asset quality crossed a supervisory boundary. A funding flag says the liability structure may be exposed to rollover or withdrawal. Neither statement proves the eventual outcome; both can tell a risk team what evidence to demand next.

For Altico, the useful question is which lens spoke first and which stayed silent. The answer above is more valuable than a blended retrospective score because it preserves responsibility. A ratio model should not take credit for a funding signal, and a funding model should not claim to have seen fabricated assets.

## The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case is the historical construction itself. A period-end metric is not necessarily what a decision-maker saw on that date. Later amendments may overwrite the original. A fixed filing-lag proxy is conservative about immediate availability but cannot reconstruct every revision. That makes this a mechanism diagnostic, not proof of live foresight.

The record's fraud-masked flag for this case is ****. If true, honest-looking published ratios can be a false negative for any disclosure-based engine. If false, the absence of a signal can still be a real miss. LiquiLens keeps both categories visible because removing them would turn research into marketing.

## What today's board shares

Today's board contains **0 red, 0 orange, 1 yellow and 2 green** rows. That is not evidence that any current institution is “the next Altico.” No similarity model is asserted here. The legitimate connection is methodological: current filings, market prices, regulatory distance and funding coverage still arrive on different clocks and can still disagree.

The board also excludes **35** stale dossiers from current presentation. That abstention is part of the signal. An institution missing from the current table is not thereby safe; it may simply lack a fresh vetted record.

## The next falsifiable test

For a current name, record the filing period, knowledge-time proxy and market date before reading the tier. Then ask whether a newer filing confirms the same asset-quality, capital or funding direction. If it reverses, the old screen should fall. If a dark funding lens becomes observable, grade whether it confirms or contradicts the tier. If the model cannot state what would change its mind, the historical lesson has not been learned.

## Follow the pressure chain

[Seiche](https://seiche.info/articles/) asks whether system funding capacity is tightening. [LiquiLens](https://liquilens.in/articles/) asks which institution balance sheet would transmit that pressure. [Undertow](https://liquilens-undertow.com/articles/) asks whether the risk can be exited in traded markets. The three layers may disagree, and that disagreement is often the finding.

articles.headline: Sambandh Finserve’s funding flag was an early disclosure signal, not a forecast
articles.dek: A historical replay places Sambandh Finserve’s first fragile funding signal before its recorded default. The evidence identifies a disclosed wholesale-leverage vulnerability, while fraud masking and construction-PIT timing limit what that chronology can establish.
articles.body_markdown:
*This is a historical replay, not current news. It is not a forecast, a credit rating, or investment advice. The filing period discussed below ended on 2016-03-31; the knowledge-time proxy is 2016-05-30. Sambandh Finserve’s recorded default date is 2020-10-13.*

The narrow answer to LiquiLens’s desk question is that Sambandh Finserve was the balance sheet that warranted earlier scrutiny because a disclosed funding measure crossed the published fragile threshold. That is not a claim that the filing predicted default, identified its cause, or created a tradeable warning. It is a claim about what the disclosed liability structure showed under a stated rule before the recorded event.

The funding lens placed Sambandh Finserve at 78.7, in the fragile band, for the period ending 2016-03-31. Its recorded flag was wholesale leverage of 8.51x against a 7x threshold. The replay calculates a 52-month lead to the recorded default. That interval is a reconstructed filing-period chronology using a knowledge-time proxy. It is neither a market-price signal nor a model-derived probability of failure.

## The record before the event

The first funding signal belongs to the 2016-03-31 reporting period and is treated as known on 2016-05-30. Where an explicit publication clock is unavailable, the construction uses period end plus 60 days. That is more cautious than assuming a balance-sheet date was instantly available, but it remains a proxy rather than a verified contemporaneous information set.

The record is classified as `PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT`. It is not eligible for validated backtesting, is not eligible for real-money use, and has no bitemporal input contract. Potential lead times may therefore be optimistic. The 52-month result is best read as a reconstructed chronology of a disclosed ratio, not evidence that a lender or investor could have acted with the same timing, information, or confidence.

A more serious limitation is that Sambandh Finserve is fraud-masked. The dossier warns that institutions whose filings were later shown to be falsified can appear compliant to a threshold engine. A mechanical screen cannot retrieve undisclosed facts or correct untruthful disclosures. This makes the case useful for testing the limits of a visible funding flag, but unsuitable for claiming that the flag explained, detected, or forecast the eventual outcome.

The underlying materials are available through the [failure-radar board](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/board), the dedicated [Sambandh Finserve replay](https://liquilens.in/replay/sambandh-finserve/), and the broader [replay archive](https://liquilens.in/replay/).

## What the lenses saw

The funding lens saw wholesale leverage above its published threshold. That is a filing-period observation: a rule applied to a disclosed liability-side measure. It is not evidence of observed lender behaviour, refinancing prices, or market consensus. It also is not a model derivation of a calibrated failure likelihood.

The PCA lens does not provide an earlier action-zone finding for Sambandh Finserve. No first action zone or related lead period is recorded. That absence cannot be converted into evidence that the institution was safe, that supervisory thresholds cleared it, or that the funding lens was sufficient on its own.

Across the replay, the PCA summary covers 15 failed institutions; 5 entered an action zone first, with a median lead of 41 months. The funding summary also covers 15 failed institutions, but liability disclosures exist for only 10. The funding signal fired first for 4, with a median lead of 38 months. These are descriptive results from a restricted disclosure record, not prospective validation. The [historical validation record](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/validation) retains those restrictions.

The India diagnostic covers 48 institutions across two decades and reports 88.9% of non-fraud failures flagged, with a median lead of 21.5 months. It carries the same construction-PIT, non-real-money, and non-validated limitations. Sambandh’s fraud-masked status matters especially because the headline excludes the category in which disclosure-based thresholds can be most misleading.

## Why the warning mattered

Wholesale leverage matters because it raises a balance-sheet question about refinancing dependence. If asset performance weakens, earnings and capital capacity may be less able to absorb losses. Where wholesale liabilities are important, funding terms and rollover willingness may become more consequential. That is a plausible pressure chain, not an established account of what happened at Sambandh.

The flag therefore mattered as a prompt for harder investigation of funding concentration, maturity structure, liquidity resilience, lender diversity, and loss-absorption capacity. The fragile label does not demonstrate that a lender withdrew, repriced, shortened, or refused funding. The dossier supplies a threshold flag, not lender-by-lender rollover evidence, cash-flow history, or a verified transmission sequence.

This distinction is essential. A filing signal can reveal a disclosed structural exposure. A market-price signal would require authorized evidence of repricing or drawdown. Neither establishes causation. A model derivation would require an eligible prospective framework able to translate inputs into a validated probability. This record explicitly does not meet that standard.

## The strongest counter-case

The counter-case can defeat an overconfident thesis. Wholesale funding is not inherently fatal. An institution can carry substantial wholesale liabilities while asset quality, capital capacity, liquidity buffers, maturities, funding diversity, and lender relationships remain resilient. A ratio threshold is a coarse representation of a more complex balance sheet.

The historical model evidence is not decisive either. The hazard panel contains 205 rows, 9 events, and 27 institutions, while 179 censored or unusable rows were excluded. Its leave-one-institution-out AUC is 0.752, with a 95% interval from 0.338 to 1.0. The heuristic comparator reports 0.799 on the same held-out rows. The temporal diagnostic AUC is 0.645, below the 0.65 gate, and remains diagnostic only.

A sceptic can reasonably conclude that the flag marked a broad vulnerability rather than a dependable countdown. Fraud masking intensifies the objection: incomplete or false disclosures can make the relationship between reported leverage and actual condition unknowable. The defensible conclusion is limited to this: Sambandh’s disclosed funding profile justified more investigation than a comparable profile without the flag.

## What today's board shares

The current board is separately dated 2026-10-20 and does not present Sambandh as a current scored row. It contains 1 yellow institution and 2 green institutions. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow at 77.8; Annapurna Finance Private Limited is green at 96.5; Arohan Financial Services Limited is green at 97.1. Each row is as of 2026-03-31 and aged 7 months.

The board excludes 35 stale institutions. It does not present quarterly filings older than 183 days or annual filings older than 400 days as current. Institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design rather than scored from memory. Those eligibility rules matter as much as the visible rows.

The market pack is fresh as of 2026-10-16, but it has no admission, publication, signal, or tier authority. Rights and display approvals are absent, and admitted canonical records are 0/25. It cannot supply market-price confirmation for this article. See the [market-evidence endpoint](https://api.liquilens.in/api/evidence/markets).

## The next falsifiable test

The thesis weakens if prospectively timestamped, vetted disclosures show flagged institutions retaining refinancing access, liquidity resilience, and loss-absorption capacity through stress while comparable unflagged institutions deteriorate first. It strengthens only if original filing vintages, explicit publication clocks, liability composition, and later outcomes are preserved before results are known.

That test cannot be satisfied by extending a retrospective replay. It requires a pre-specified prospective cohort and evaluation that does not inherit revised knowledge from later filings or outcomes.

## Follow the pressure chain

LiquiLens covers **institution and lender balance-sheet risk**. Seiche covers **system dollar-funding capacity**. Undertow covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity. These are distinct analytical objects, not interchangeable confirmations.

The [LiquiLens research archive](https://liquilens.in/research/) provides institution-focused context. The [Seiche overview](https://api.seiche.info/api/overview) is system context only here. The [Undertow board](https://api.seiche.info/undertow/board.json) addresses exit capacity, not Sambandh’s historical funding flag. System strain or market illiquidity cannot replace missing institutional disclosures or turn a filing replay into a forecast.

## Sources, method, and limits

This article uses the supplied LiquiLens record only: the [failure-radar board](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/board), [historical validation](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/validation), [market evidence](https://api.liquilens.in/api/evidence/markets), and [Sambandh replay](https://liquilens.in/replay/sambandh-finserve/).

The decisive limitations are the period-end-plus-60-days availability proxy, absent bitemporal input control, potentially optimistic lead times, missing liability disclosures, fraud masking, and the absence of authorized market-derived display or tier evidence. The finding is not that Sambandh’s end was forecast. It is that a disclosed funding vulnerability appeared early enough to warrant harder questions, while the record remains too constrained to claim more.

Research and market data, not investment advice.

This is not a credit rating.

articles.body_markdown:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. It examines New India Co-operative Bank around its 2025-02-13 event date. Similar mechanisms do not imply the same outcome elsewhere.*

The narrow answer to the desk question is New India Co-operative Bank: disclosed balance-sheet stress appeared first in the asset-quality lens. The replay records an RBI action-zone breach for NNPA in FY2021, for the period ending 2021-03-31. Its assigned knowledge-time proxy is 2021-05-30, and the recorded lead is 44 months.

That finding requires careful classification. It is a filing-period signal: a breach derived from a reported period, with availability assigned by an explicit publication clock when available or by period end plus 60 days otherwise. It is not a market-price signal, and it is not a model-derived probability of failure. The record is fraud-masked and labelled `PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT`; it is not validated-backtest eligible, not real-money eligible, and has no bitemporal input contract. The dossier says its lead times are optimistic.

## The record before the event

The first action-zone observation was FY2021. The listed breach was NNPA. The replay links the 2021-05-30 knowledge-time proxy to the 2021-03-31 period end, before the 2025-02-13 event. This supports a limited sequencing claim: the disclosed asset-quality screen fired before the recorded event.

The funding lens did not provide an earlier result. New India’s funding record is scoreable, but no first funding signal or funding lead is reported. This is missing signal evidence, not affirmative evidence of calm funding. The funding lens can assess only institutions that disclose a liability series. The absence of an earlier disclosed funding flag does not establish that deposits, liquidity, or other liabilities were free from pressure.

The fraud-masked designation is material. A threshold engine sees reported inputs rather than concealed conditions. The dossier notes that filings later shown falsified can look compliant to a threshold engine, with the forensic screen owning that limitation. A public-disclosure replay cannot convert a reported ratio into proof of institutional condition, solvency, or safety.

## What the lenses saw

The regulatory lens observed an NNPA breach. The funding lens did not establish an earlier disclosed signal. That is the complete supported ordering. It permits the conclusion that asset-quality deterioration was the earliest visible warning in this replay. It does not support the stronger claim that funding was sound, irrelevant, or later in the institution’s underlying condition.

Across the historical summaries, lenses do not have a universal order. Of 15 failed institutions in the PCA/SAF summary, 5 entered the action zone first, with median lead of 41 months. Of those 15, 10 had liability disclosures in the funding summary; funding fired first for 4, with median lead of 38 months. The funding lens did not produce an earlier competing signal because the institution was not scoreable under that lens.

That is a sequence, not a complete explanation of failure. A filing-period signal says that a disclosed condition was recorded for a reporting period. A knowledge-time proxy estimates when that condition could have been known. A market-price signal, by contrast, is a contemporaneous repricing measure. A model derivation turns available inputs into a rule, score, or tier. Confusing those categories can make a historical replay sound more predictive than the evidence permits.

The relevant research boundary is explicit: **PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT** evidence is not a validated backtest and is not real-money-eligible. The institution-risk boundary is equally explicit: LiquiLens covers **institution and lender balance-sheet risk**. The reconstruction assigns **1999-05-30** as the knowledge-time proxy, using the stated period-end-plus-**60-day** convention where no explicit publication clock is available. The reported lead to default is **41 months**.

These dates serve different purposes. **1999-03-31** is a filing-period endpoint, not proof that market participants knew the result that day. **1999-05-30** is a conservative availability proxy, not a verified publication timestamp. **2002-11-02** is the default date. The distinction is material: the reported lead depends on the availability convention, and the dossier says lead times are optimistic.

The [Nedungadi Bank replay](https://liquilens.in/replay/nedungadi-bank/) and the [Failure Radar board](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/board) support only the narrow finding that CRAR was the first action-zone breach captured in this reconstruction. A capital breach matters because it identifies reduced loss-absorbing room under a supervisory framework. In mechanism terms, less capital capacity can constrain management options, sharpen supervisory attention, and make confidence more consequential. Funding pressure may then follow, or may become observable only later.

Nedungadi supports that conditional mechanism only in a limited sense. The capital breach is observed. The funding lens is unavailable. This is also why the absence of a funding alert cannot be read as an all-clear. “Unscoreable” is not “safe.” It means there is no eligible funding inference from the disclosed series. The distinction is the core editorial lesson of the case.

## The strongest counter-case

The counter-case is strong enough to defeat any deterministic thesis. ## What today's board shares

## The next falsifiable test

The thesis fails if prospectively time-stamped filings show that capital action-zone breaches add no earlier or more useful warning than eligible funding disclosures, forensic evidence, or other published components. The products answer distinct questions. LiquiLens addresses **institution and lender balance-sheet risk** through [LiquiLens investigations](https://liquilens.in/investigations/). articles.headline: Madhavpura replay: the warning a disclosure screen could not honestly give
articles.dek: Madhavpura Mercantile Co-operative Bank is classified as fraud-masked. Its record does not establish an early warning from either the PCA-style or funding lens; it establishes a boundary between reported filings, market prices, and model output.
articles.body_markdown:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. Similar mechanisms do not imply the same outcome. Madhavpura Mercantile Co-operative Bank’s recorded default date is 2012-06-04; this article was published on 2026-10-17.*

Madhavpura Mercantile Co-operative Bank presents the hardest version of LiquiLens’s desk question: which institution balance sheet should feel financial stress first, and why? The honest answer cannot be manufactured from an incomplete record. The dossier classifies Madhavpura as fraud-masked, records no PCA first action-zone date or lead-month measure, and says the funding lens is not scoreable.

That does not mean the institution was sound before its recorded default. Nor does it show that a public disclosure model detected the problem late. It means the supplied evidence does not support either claim. A filing-period signal describes what an eligible disclosed record produced. A market-price signal describes repricing in a market series. A model derivation combines admitted inputs under stated rules. None can repair a compromised or unavailable institution-level disclosure record.

## The record before the event

Madhavpura is classified as an urban co-operative bank, with a recorded default date of 2012-06-04. The dossier marks it fraud-masked. No institution-specific filing as-of date is supplied. That absence matters: a missing publication or filing date cannot be converted into proof that the reported position was stable, timely, or representative of the economic position.

The PCA replay records no first action-zone breach and no measured lead for Madhavpura. The funding lens is explicitly not scoreable, with no first signal and no lead time. Those are eligibility and observability results, not negative findings on financial stress.

The framework’s method note identifies the central problem directly: an institution whose filings were later shown to have been falsified can appear compliant to a threshold engine. In that circumstance, the apparent filing result concerns the disclosed record, not necessarily the underlying balance sheet. The forensic screen, rather than a ratio threshold, owns that limitation.

The [Madhavpura replay](https://liquilens.in/replay/madhavpura-mercantile-co-operative-bank/) and the [failure-radar board](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/board) retain the classification without inventing a pre-event chronology. That restraint is the point. Nothing in the dossier permits an assertion that Madhavpura cleared a stress test, escaped a warning, or had no funding pressure.

## What the lenses saw

The PCA lens supplies no usable first-warning sequence for this institution. It is a filing-period lens: its relevant observation is whether disclosed and eligible inputs meet an action-zone rule. For Madhavpura, the dossier does not report the first action-zone date or a lead-month measure. There is therefore no institution-specific PCA timing claim to make.

The funding lens is even more limited. It is not scoreable because the required liability disclosure series was unavailable to that lens. An unscoreable funding result is not evidence of secure funding. It says that the model’s required input was not available in a form that made the institution eligible for the calculation.

Neither result is a market-price signal. The record supplies no admitted Madhavpura market-price measure, drawdown, or market-derived tier. A market price, where properly authorized, could show investor repricing; it would not by itself verify the balance-sheet condition. Here, it is absent as institution-specific evidence.

The wider historical summaries are useful context but cannot be used to fill Madhavpura’s missing fields. In the funding summary, 15 failed institutions are included, 10 have liability disclosures, 4 had the funding signal fire first, and median lead is 38 months. The warning in this replay is methodological rather than predictive. A reported capital, asset-quality, liquidity, or funding measure is an observation from a filing-period record. It is not automatically a verified statement about the economic balance sheet. Where the disclosed record is compromised, a threshold result can be accurately calculated and still fail to describe the underlying condition.

It cannot transform an unscoreable funding series into a calm funding finding, and it cannot interpret an unreported PCA event date as evidence that no stress existed.

That is why fraud masking must remain visible. Folding such cases into a simple success or failure count would exaggerate what the screen observed. Madhavpura is not evidence that the PCA lens warned first, that funding warned first, or that either lens had a measured lead. It is evidence that disclosure integrity comes before any model claim.

## The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case can defeat an overbroad thesis: disclosure screens should not be expected to reveal information that was concealed, unavailable, or not eligible for their rules. Their performance should be judged on the disclosed records they can actually observe.

There is supportive, but bounded, evidence for usefulness in observable cases. The India evidence index covers 48 institutions across two decades and reports 88.9% of non-fraud failures flagged, with median lead of 21.5 months. Yet the same evidence is identified as a filing-availability-proxied construction-PIT diagnostic. It is not validated-backtest eligible, not real-money eligible, and does not have a bitemporal input contract.

Where an explicit publication clock is unavailable, the construction uses period end plus 60 days. The dossier explicitly says lead times are optimistic. That qualification can defeat any claim that the reported lead is equivalent to a tradable or contemporaneously knowable warning. The PCA and funding summaries therefore demonstrate conditional historical signal behavior, not a clean real-time record and not a Madhavpura-specific detection.

The counter-case is stronger than a disclaimer: public disclosures may be useful when disclosures are credible and eligible, while being unable to penetrate a fraud-masked record. Madhavpura does not disprove the lenses. It does disprove the claim that their non-signal was reassuring.

This interpretation would weaken if preserved pre-default disclosures established that Madhavpura crossed the PCA-style action zone before 2012-06-04. It would also weaken if a qualifying liability series produced an earlier funding signal under the stated rule. Either result would create a measured institution-specific lead that the current dossier does not provide.

The opposite result would also be informative. If the historical record continued to contain no usable eligible disclosures for either lens, fraud masking and missing eligibility would remain the better explanation for the non-signal. That would not establish that every fraud-masked institution behaves alike. It would preserve the narrower claim about this case and this record.

The required sequence is disclosure integrity, lens eligibility, filing-period signal, model derivation, authority, and only then an institution-risk conclusion. Madhavpura breaks that chain at disclosure integrity and funding eligibility. A non-reported PCA timing field and an unscoreable funding field cannot be recast as a calm balance sheet.

LiquiLens covers **institution and lender balance-sheet risk**. Seiche covers **system dollar-funding capacity**. Undertow covers **market liquidity and executable exit capacity**. Those are distinct research boundaries, not interchangeable evidence categories. The [Seiche overview](https://api.seiche.info/api/overview) and the [Undertow board](https://api.seiche.info/undertow/board.json) can provide separate system or exit context, but cannot substitute for Madhavpura’s missing institution-level evidence.

It does not establish that asset quality caused the default, that markets ignored a known fact, or that the interval was tradable. The distinction matters. The [United Western Bank replay](https://liquilens.in/replay/united-western-bank/) identifies the first PCA action-zone observation as `threshold_2`, with NNPA as the breach, at 2001-03-31. That produces the 2001-05-30 knowledge-time proxy and a stated lead of 63 months to the 2006-09-02 default.

That lead is useful only if read correctly. The period end says when the reported condition is assigned in the replay. The proxy says when the process assumes that condition could have been known. The historical summaries are similarly constrained. Of 15 failed institutions, five first entered an action zone, with a median lead of 41 months. The funding lens had liability disclosures for 10 of the 15, fired first for four, and had a median lead of 38 months. Market-derived display and tier conclusions are therefore not authorized here. A filing signal cannot be recast as a market-price signal merely because market data exist elsewhere in the product.

It is therefore inappropriate to treat 1999-03-31 as a verified real-time observation date.

The funding lens supplies no offsetting result. Nedungadi is marked unscoreable for funding, with no first signal and no measured funding lead. That does not show that funding was stable. The case therefore separates three things that are too easily blended. The strongest counter-case can defeat a stronger version of the thesis. The funding lens saw a disclosed liability mix: commercial paper represented 29% at the cited period end. A lender dependent on repeated issuance has a specific vulnerability if refinancing becomes unavailable. It may need replacement cash or other balance-sheet actions under time pressure.

The PCA/SAF lens replays public disclosure against the RBI’s action-zone tripwires. The [New India replay](https://liquilens.in/replay/new-india-co-operative-bank/) is evidence of what a disclosure screen could flag from the available record.

Fraud-masked is not a footnote. Institutions whose filings were later shown falsified can appear compliant to a threshold engine. Timing is another objection. The replay uses explicit publication time when present and otherwise a period-end-plus-60-days proxy. That can make lead times optimistic. The conformal alarm is diagnostic, with no score or tier authority pending prospective revalidation.

A later event also does not retroactively prove decision usefulness. The heuristic’s stronger held-out AUC and the failed temporal gate limit the model conclusion. articles.dek: A historical replay places Nedungadi Bank in an RBI action zone on its FY1999 CRAR disclosure before default. It is a filing-period signal under a proxy clock, not a market-price warning or a calibrated forecast.
articles.body_markdown:

Nedungadi Bank should have appeared under pressure first through disclosed capital, not through a scored funding signal. The narrow thesis is that its CRAR entry into the first RBI action zone in FY1999 was the earliest observable warning in this replay. It preceded the bank’s 2002-11-02 default by 41 months. That does not prove capital caused the default, establish what market participants knew, or show that an investor could have traded a known outcome.

The distinction is central. The CRAR breach is a filing-period signal, subject to an availability proxy. A market-price signal would require authorised market evidence, and none establishes Nedungadi’s historical pathway. A model derivation is a rule or diagnostic built over observed records; it is not itself an observed event. Conflating these categories would turn a limited replay into a claim it cannot support.

This historical replay is **not investment advice** and **not a credit rating**.

## The record before the event

The [Nedungadi Bank replay](https://liquilens.in/replay/nedungadi-bank/) records its first PCA/SAF action-zone entry at the 1999-03-31 period end, labelled FY1999. The breach was CRAR and its status was `threshold_1`. The knowledge-time proxy is 1999-05-30, using the stated 60-day filing lag. The [Failure Radar board](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/board) preserves that separation rather than silently treating period-end information as immediately known.

Nedungadi is marked as not fraud-masked. That means this replay does not assign it to the group in which filings later shown to be falsified can make an institution appear compliant to a threshold engine. It does not establish that disclosed information was complete.

## What the lenses saw

The PCA lens saw the CRAR breach. The funding lens was not scoreable and produced no first signal. This is a missing-data outcome, not a conclusion that funding was calm, stable, or irrelevant. The funding framework can observe only institutions disclosing a liability series; Nedungadi’s record does not support that lens.

The rule-based `threshold_1` classification is also not a market price. The 41-month lead is a model derivation from a proxy knowledge date and a recorded default date. Neither converts an action-zone breach into a calibrated failure frequency.

## The strongest counter-case

A stronger version of this thesis can fail. One action-zone breach in a construction-PIT record may identify regulatory vulnerability while revealing little about timing, severity, or the eventual failure mechanism. A 41-month lead itself argues against interpreting the result as an imminent-event alarm.

The availability convention may flatter apparent warning time. The record lacks a bitemporal input contract and substitutes period end plus 60 days where no explicit publication clock exists. If fully timestamped, contemporaneous liability information had generated an earlier warning, the claim that capital should feel stress first would fail. If a market-price measure had repriced before the filing became knowable, it would answer a different question and also defeat any claim that the filing was the first observable warning overall. The defensible conclusion is narrower: capital was the earliest recorded signal in this replay.

## What today's board shares

Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange on a 2025-03-31 dossier. Belstar Microfinance Limited and ESAF Small Finance Bank are yellow.

These are published-rule screens over vetted public dossiers, not ratings. Yet the current market layer has 0 of 25 admitted canonical records and has no tier or publication authority. It is fresh and clocked, but display and tier use are not approved. The [market evidence endpoint](https://api.liquilens.in/api/evidence/markets) records that boundary.

The thesis weakens if a prospective, fully timestamped filing record shows that action-zone entry does not precede meaningful balance-sheet stress more reliably than available alternatives when disclosure timing is held constant. It also weakens if institutions with disclosed liability series repeatedly generate earlier usable funding warnings and CRAR adds no incremental diagnostic value.

That test must use actual publication timestamps rather than period-end proxies, preserve missing disclosures as missing, and separate forensic cases in which filings can mask weakness. Until then, this remains a historically grounded mechanism claim, not a calibrated forecast.

## Follow the pressure chain

The pressure chain supported here stops at disclosed CRAR weakness, RBI action-zone entry, and eventual default. The funding link is unobserved, not absent. No market-price link is established.

The product boundaries matter: Seiche covers **system dollar-funding capacity**; LiquiLens covers **institution and lender balance-sheet risk**; Undertow covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity. Seiche’s composite is 41.2 and labelled EROSION, with guarded confidence because slow-moving or modelled structure has not been broadly confirmed by current market plumbing. See the [Seiche overview](https://api.seiche.info/api/overview) and [Undertow board](https://api.seiche.info/undertow/board.json).

The decisive limits are construction-PIT historical status, no real-money eligibility, no bitemporal input contract, proxy timing that can leave lead times optimistic, no authorised market-derived tier evidence, and unscoreable funding evidence for Nedungadi. articles.headline: First Leasing replay: when a public balance-sheet radar cannot see through the record
articles.dek: First Leasing Company Of India’s fraud-masked default is not an early-warning success. It is a boundary case showing why a filing-period signal, a market-price signal and a model derivation must not be treated as the same evidence.
articles.body_markdown:
*Historical replay — not current news and not a forecast.* First Leasing Company Of India defaulted on 2013-12-02. The useful lesson is not that a public screen called the event. The supplied record does not establish that it did. Rather, it shows a harder limitation: an institution can be under severe economic pressure while its reported balance sheet fails to transmit that pressure to a threshold-based public-data system.

The distinction matters for the desk question: which balance sheet should feel stress first, and why? A filing-period signal describes what disclosed reports showed at an available reporting point. A market-price signal describes repricing in tradable instruments, when the market data are authorized for that use. A model derivation combines permitted inputs under a stated rule. None can be silently substituted for another; none proves the underlying economic condition by itself.

First Leasing is marked `fraud_masked` in this replay. Its case therefore tests the boundary of disclosed-data surveillance, rather than supplying evidence that an ordinary balance-sheet deterioration was identified in time.

## The record before the event

First Leasing Company Of India is classified as an NBFC, with default date 2013-12-02. Its PCA record contains no first action-zone date and no lead-month figure. Its funding record is scoreable, but contains no first signal and no lead-month figure. These are missing replay results, not affirmative findings that funding was calm, capital was adequate or the institution was safe.

The historical framework explicitly warns that institutions whose filings were later shown falsified can look compliant to a threshold engine; the forensic screen owns those cases. That warning is central here. The dossier does not provide underlying accounting particulars that would establish the route from misstatement to default. It does establish that the reported public record did not produce an earlier PCA action-zone entry or funding signal in this replay.

The India evidence is broader but tightly qualified. It covers 48 institutions across two decades, with a headline finding that 88.9% of non-fraud failures were flagged and median lead was 21.5 months. Yet its status is `PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT`: it is not validated-backtest eligible, not real-money eligible and has no bitemporal input contract. Availability uses an explicit publication clock when present; otherwise it uses period end plus 60 days. The dossier says lead times are optimistic. These are diagnostic construction results, not tradable performance evidence. See the [Failure Radar board](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/board), [validation record](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/validation) and [First Leasing replay](https://liquilens.in/replay/first-leasing-company-of-india/).

## What the lenses saw

The PCA lens is a public-disclosure replay of the RBI’s PCA/SAF tripwires. Among 15 failed institutions, 5 entered an action zone first, with median lead of 41 months. That is evidence that disclosed supervisory-style thresholds can be informative in some cases. It is not evidence that they identified First Leasing: its supplied PCA fields show no action-zone date and no lead time.

The funding lens is narrower because it requires a disclosed liability series. Of 15 failed institutions, 10 had liability disclosures; the funding signal fired first for 4, with median lead of 38 months. First Leasing is marked scoreable, yet no first funding signal is recorded. That is a non-result in the replay, not a clean bill of health.

A filing-period signal must also be separated from a model derivation. The published rule can fuse disclosed levels, deterioration, a funding flag, a forensic indicator and an authoritative market drawdown into a presentation tier. PD levels are corpus-fitted and prior-corrected to a ~0.25%/yr population base rate using King-Zeng. That makes them model outputs, not direct observations. The conformal alarm is retained only as a diagnostic: its historical tier wiring is suspended and it has no score or tier authority pending prospective revalidation.

A market-price signal is different again. The dossier describes Merton PD as a market repricing signal, not a calibrated failure frequency. For the current market layer, data are fresh and clocked, but display, model-gate and tier use are not approved; admitted canonical records are 0/25. Market information therefore cannot authorize a current tier in this record.

## Why the warning mattered

A reported balance sheet is supposed to connect asset quality, loss absorption and creditor confidence. If losses, impairment or other relevant conditions are not truthfully represented, reported capital and risk measures can remain clear of a threshold. If disclosure does not reveal why liability providers should reassess the institution, a funding lens may not fire either.

That is an inference about the limits of observable inputs, not a reconstructed account of First Leasing’s finances. The dossier supports the narrower conclusion: in a fraud-masked case, apparent compliance in disclosed data may be an artefact of the record rather than evidence of resilience. A missed signal in an honest, timely disclosure regime could challenge the threshold. A missed signal where filings were later shown falsified can instead show that the measured balance sheet was not a reliable map of the institution.

## The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case can defeat any inflated version of this thesis. Perhaps the framework is simply too weak to identify stress reliably. First Leasing has no recorded PCA or funding lead. Historical availability is sometimes proxied using period end plus 60 days, and the dossier expressly calls the lead times optimistic.

The hazard evidence is also limited. The panel has 205 rows, 9 events and 27 institutions; 179 censored or unusable rows were excluded. Leave-one-institution-out AUC is 0.752, with an interval of 0.338 to 1.0. On the same held-out rows, the heuristic AUC is 0.799, above the hazard AUC. The temporal test has AUC of 0.645, below the 0.65 diagnostic gate, and cannot promote construction-PIT diagnostics.

That critique means this replay cannot demonstrate that the radar would have protected a creditor, investor or supervisor. Nor can a `fraud_masked` label solve forensic identification after the fact. The defensible claim is smaller: the system reports the absence and limits of disclosed signals rather than converting unavailable or compromised evidence into reassurance.

## What today's board shares

The board as of 2026-09-25 has 0 red institutions, 1 orange, 3 yellow and 15 green; 21 stale institutions are excluded. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange, based on a 2025-03-31 filing as-of date aged 18 months, with score 74.9. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow as of 2026-03-31, aged 6 months, score 77.8. Nothing older than 24 months is presented as current, while institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design. The current market layer is as of 2026-09-24, but lacks publication and tier authority. ## The next falsifiable test

The thesis weakens if a genuinely bitemporal, prospectively audited sample finds that disclosed PCA, funding and forensic signals do not identify pressure before adverse outcomes better than chance. It gains credibility only if prospective records preserve what was knowable when, retain missing and stale observations instead of filling them with calm, and separately test filing signals, market-price signals and model derivations. This is not investment advice and not a credit rating.

## Follow the pressure chain

The disciplined sequence is reported assets and capital; disclosed liability structure; supervisory-style thresholds; forensic indicators; then market and exit conditions where authority permits. A break should prompt investigation, not automatic certainty.

LiquiLens covers **institution and lender balance-sheet risk**. [Seiche](https://api.seiche.info/api/overview) covers **system dollar-funding capacity**. ## The next falsifiable test

The thesis fails if a genuinely prospective dataset with publication timestamps finds that these screens do not identify later pressure within their stated limits, or if apparent leads disappear after replacing the period-end-plus-60-day proxy with actual availability. It also fails for this replay if newly eligible primary disclosures establish a materially different chronology.

The test should freeze rules before outcomes, preserve publication times, retain unavailable fields as unavailable, and assess signals only after the forward observation horizon closes. Until then, historical leads remain diagnostic. This is not investment advice.

## Follow the pressure chain

The research boundary is explicit. LiquiLens addresses **institution and lender balance-sheet risk**. [Seiche](https://api.seiche.info/api/overview) addresses **system dollar-funding capacity**. [Undertow](https://api.seiche.info/undertow/board.json) addresses market liquidity and executable exit capacity.

Those are different questions. Seiche’s current read can describe a divergence that warrants investigation without proving an institution squeeze. Undertow can describe partial market coverage without determining a lender’s disclosed capital condition. Conversely, an institution filing screen can justify further work even when market-derived data lack tier authority. The [Undertow board](https://api.seiche.info/undertow/board.json) and [LiquiLens investigations](https://liquilens.in/investigations/) should be treated as distinct analytical handoffs, not confirming votes.

## Sources, method, and limits

This article uses only the supplied evidence universe: the [board](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/board), [historical validation](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/validation), [market evidence](https://api.liquilens.in/api/evidence/markets), [Rupee replay](https://liquilens.in/replay/rupee-co-operative-bank/), and [LiquiLens research](https://liquilens.in/research/).

The central limitation is substantive: this is a period-end-proxy construction with a 60-day fallback filing lag and optimistic historical lead times. Missing liability data are not evidence of stable funding. A missing action-zone date is not evidence that pressure was absent. A visible market layer can still lack admission, publication, and tier authority. Rupee Co-operative Bank is therefore a warning about evidentiary boundaries: a balance-sheet screen can sharpen an investigation, but it cannot create the missing proof of sequence.
